nameStory: The Green Long-jawed Orbweaver gets its name from two standout features that make it easy to remember. Its vibrant green coloration helps it blend seamlessly with the leafy plants where it hunts, while its dramatically elongated jaws (called chelicerae) stretch forward like tiny green chopsticks. The 'orbweaver' part comes from the classic circular webs these spiders craft, though this species often abandons web-building for active hunting.
description: The Green Long-jawed Orbweaver is a slender, bright green spider that looks almost like a tiny green stick with legs. Its most striking feature is its extremely long, forward-projecting jaws that can be nearly as long as its body. These spiders typically measure about 6-10mm in body length, with long, thin legs that help them navigate through grass and low vegetation. Their brilliant green color makes them masters of camouflage among plants.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated, pencil-thin body with a narrow abdomen that feels almost twig-like if gently touched

idTips.label: Jaws
idTips.description: Dramatically long, forward-projecting chelicerae (jaws) that extend like green chopsticks and are nearly as long as the body itself

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright apple-green to yellow-green coloration that perfectly matches fresh vegetation, sometimes with a subtle metallic sheen

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: May build small, irregular orb webs in vegetation, but often hunts actively without a web, moving with deliberate, stick-like motions

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: When threatened, stretches out completely straight along plant stems, becoming nearly invisible and feeling rigid like a small twig

habitat: Green Long-jawed Orbweavers thrive in moist areas with dense vegetation, particularly along pond edges, stream banks, and wetland margins throughout New England. They prefer tall grasses, cattails, and herbaceous plants where their green coloration provides perfect camouflage. You'll often find them in gardens, meadows, and anywhere lush green vegetation grows thick.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring as vegetation greens up, with their bright coloration perfectly matching fresh plant growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting among dense vegetation and occasionally building webs.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced, though adults may remain active well into autumn if temperatures stay mild.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off with hard frosts, while eggs overwinter to hatch the following spring.

funFact: When hunting, Green Long-jawed Orbweavers can actually change their posture to mimic different parts of plants - they'll stretch out straight to look like a stem, or huddle up to resemble a leaf bud, making them some of nature's most convincing plant impersonators.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other green Tetragnatha species, but the bright apple-green color (rather than yellowish or pale green) and the perfectly straight posture when hiding help distinguish this species. Remember: 'vivid viridis' - the most intensely green of the stretch spiders.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'viridis' literally means 'green' in Latin, making this one of the more straightforward spider names to remember. Unlike many orbweavers that are completely dependent on their webs, these spiders represent an evolutionary transition toward active hunting.
compareHints: Among its Tetragnatha relatives, the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out with its vivid green coloration, while the Common Stretch Spider tends to be more yellowish or brownish, and the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver has distinctive metallic silver markings. All stretch spiders share the elongated jaws and thin body shape, but viridis is typically the most intensely colored green of the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's long-jawed orbweavers, the Common Stretch Spider is distinguished by its extreme elongation and distinctive straight-line defensive posture.
Among its stretch spider relatives, the Elongate Stilt Spider has the most extreme body elongation - much more stretched than the Common Stretch Spider or Green Long-jawed Orbweaver.
Unlike the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver that stays near water and has greenish coloring, versicolor prefers dry areas and shows yellow-orange tones.

Among the Tetragnatha genus in New England, the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out for its distinctive metallic silvery appearance, while the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver appears more yellow-green and the Common Stretch Spider tends to be brownish.
Compared to its relatives, the Straw-colored Stretch Spider is consistently paler than the bright green T.
Unlike the Common Stretch Spider which has a more uniform abdomen, the tailed long-jawed orbweaver has that distinctive rear projection.
